lessons.situation: A tenant reports an appliance fault, the agency suggests a troubleshooting setting from the manual, and the tenant replies that the appliance has still never worked and asks for someone to inspect it.
lessons.action: When the tenant says self-help troubleshooting has failed and asks for an inspection, send a short holding reply to the tenant saying you will be back in touch. Then email the landlord asking for approval to send an appliance repair contractor to inspect, and put the job on hold awaiting the landlord's response.
lessons.rationale: Once troubleshooting is ruled out, a contractor visit needs landlord approval, and the tenant should know it is being handled without being promised a visit before that approval.

lessons.situation: The agency needed a tenant's solar panel meter reading photo for a periodic landlord record, held the task until the due period, chased the tenant by email and phone, and the tenant eventually replied with the photo attached.
lessons.action: When the tenant's reply arrives with the requested meter reading photo, forward the attachment straight to the landlord, state which period the reading covers, and ask when they will next need one. Then mark the task complete without escalating or handing off to anyone else.
lessons.rationale: The task is a simple evidence-collection loop, so once the tenant supplies the photo the quickest way to close it is to pass it to the landlord with a note on the period and the next due date.

lessons.situation: A tenant reported a door that has become hard to shut, and the landlord replied with a known workaround from past experience and proposed deferring any contractor visit.
lessons.action: Relay the landlord's workaround to the tenant by phone and ask them to try it before any contractor is booked. If it works, tell the landlord you are closing the request unless the tenant reports the problem again, and ask the tenant to come back if it recurs. Don't send a formal response chasing approval or book a contractor, and return the request to auto mode or close it.
lessons.rationale: When the landlord supplies a workable fix for a non-urgent, recurring fault and the tenant confirms it works, a contractor visit is unnecessary. Closing with a clear route to reopen keeps costs down while protecting the tenant.

lessons.situation: A tenant reported a broken key with no spare held by tenant or agency, and the landlord approved the replacement and asked for extra keys for the tenant, landlord and agency.
lessons.action: Acknowledge the landlord's approval and confirm you are arranging the work. Rewrite the job description for the provider to include the landlord's specific instructions: replace the lock, supply the exact number of new keys, and state who each set is for, including that the landlord's and agency's sets must be handed to the office. Then move to provider selection, assign the provider, and tell the tenant who will attend and that the provider will contact them to arrange a visit.
lessons.rationale: Putting the landlord's exact requirements into the provider's brief at the point of approval avoids misunderstandings over key quantities and handover, and keeps all parties informed of the next steps.

lessons.situation: A tenant asked for garden clearance, levelling and gravelling, the landlord did not respond within the chase window, and the automated process flagged the job for manual review.
lessons.action: When the landlord approval wait expires with no reply, hand the job to the responsible property manager, who should contact the landlord directly (phone or direct chase) to resolve it. Once a quote is obtained and approved, book the contractor. Before works are ordered, put the job on hold to request funds up front from the landlord to cover the invoice, and keep it on hold while waiting for the provider's start date.
lessons.rationale: Escalating a stalled approval to a named person gets a decision faster than repeated automated chasing, and securing landlord funds before works begin avoids unpaid contractor invoices.

input.body:
Hello,

Thank you for confirming this repair request is yours rather than one the landlord asked for. Please note our earlier email showed the wrong address by mistake. This request is for Flat 26, 116 Copperfield Walk, Alderwick, ZZ7 8ZZ (ref R/PM045-1).

So we can put it to your landlord, please reply with a short description of what is wrong with the kitchen window and the patio door windows (for example cracked or broken glass, condensation between the panes, a broken handle or hinge, draughts, or they won't open or close). Photos would help a lot if you can take them.

Most importantly: if the patio door or any window will not close or lock securely, or there is broken glass, please tell us straight away by phone so we can arrange an urgent visit. Until then, keep clear of any broken glass.

We will follow up in 2 working days if we haven't heard from you.

Kind regards,
Donna
Northbridge Lettings
